# Completing the Square — Find a Minimum Without Guessing

## The identity to remember

$$
x^2+2ax+a^2=(x+a)^2
$$

**Every symbol explained:** x is an unknown real number; a is a fixed real value; the left expression has a quadratic term, a linear term and a constant; the right is a perfect square.

**Substitute actual numbers:** For x²−6x+13, use a=−3: (x−3)²+4, because (x−3)²=x²−6x+9. Its minimum is 4, achieved at x=3.

## Why it is true

A real square is always nonnegative. Rewriting a quadratic as a square plus a constant exposes its smallest value and where that value occurs. It is more informative than testing many x values.

## When to recognise it

Use this in algorithm geometry, optimisation on intervals and deriving bounds on expressions. For integer x, the ideal real minimiser may not be an allowed integer, so test its nearest legal integers.

## Algorithm or number puzzle application

To minimise n²−7n+12 over integers n, rewrite (n−3.5)²−0.25. Integer n=3 or 4 both give 0.

## Assumptions and pitfalls

The argument that a square is nonnegative applies to real numbers; if optimisation has constraints, the global vertex may lie outside the feasible range.

## Your turn

Complete the square for x²+8x+20, then identify its smallest real value.

**Memory rule:** Understand the cancellation or construction that produces the identity. Re-derive the rule from two small numbers, then say aloud when you would use it.
